title: The woman taken in adultery: a story that moved
excerpt: John 7:53-8:11 is missing from the oldest copies of John and turns up in other places in later ones. What that tells us about the gospels, and what it does not.
body: It is one of the best-known scenes in the gospels. The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery, stand her in the middle of the Temple court and ask Jesus whether she should be stoned. He writes on the ground with his finger. Then he says: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7). They leave one by one, the eldest first.
Most printed Bibles still carry it. Most of them also put it in brackets, or add a footnote, because the oldest copies of John do not have it.
## What the manuscripts show
@consensus

The passage runs from John 7:53 to 8:11. It is absent from the two earliest papyri of John, P66 and P75, both usually dated to around 200 CE. It is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two great Greek Bibles of the fourth century. The first Greek manuscript to carry it is Codex Bezae, copied around 400 CE.{{fn:Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994), pages 187-189.}}

And when it does turn up, it does not always turn up in the same place. Some manuscripts put it after John 7:36. Others put it after John 21:25, at the very end of the gospel. A group of manuscripts known as family 13 puts it in Luke, after Luke 21:38.{{fn:Metzger, Textual Commentary, page 189.}}

A story that wanders between two gospels and three positions is a story that copyists were trying to find a home for. Bruce Metzger, who edited the Greek text most translations are made from, put it bluntly: “The evidence for the non-Johannine origin of the pericope of the adulteress is overwhelming.”{{fn:Metzger, Textual Commentary, page 187.}}
## Where it came from
So where did it come from? The honest answer is that the evidence runs out, and I would rather say so than pretend.

There are hints of an older story. Eusebius, writing in the early fourth century, says Papias told “a story about a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, which is contained in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.”{{fn:Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.17.}} A third-century church order, the Didascalia Apostolorum, tells a version of it to bishops as a lesson in mercy. So the story circulated before it entered John. Whether it is a memory of something Jesus did is a separate question, and the evidence does not settle it either way.
@minority

Augustine had his own theory. He suggested that some men had cut the passage out of their copies because they feared it would give their wives licence to sin.{{fn:Augustine, De adulterinis coniugiis 2.7.6.}} Metzger did not accept it, and the pattern of the evidence runs the other way: a passage added, in different places, by different hands.
## Why it matters on this site

The passage is a clean case of what the Qur’an means when it treats the scripture of the People of the Book as something that carries the revelation alongside other things. Here is a text that a reader of John in the year 300 would never have seen, now read aloud in churches as the Word of God.

I am careful here, because the Qur’an passes no verdict on this story, and I will not invent one for it. The site sorts gospel material by the measure, and on that measure this passage is unclear: nothing in it conflicts with the Qur’an, and nothing in the Qur’an confirms it. What the manuscripts show is that it was added to John, and that is a fact about the book, which is open to anyone to check.
@islamic

There is a curious echo in the hadith. Al-Bukhārī records that a group of Jews in Medina brought a man and a woman accused of adultery to the Prophet, hoping for a lighter judgement than their own law gave. He asked what the Torah said. One of them covered a verse with his hand. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām told him to lift it, and the verse of stoning was underneath.{{fn:Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-manāqib, 3635.}} The Qur’an comments on the same kind of case: “But why do they come to you for judgement when they have the Torah, in which is God’s judgement?” (5:43).

Both stories have the same shape. An accused woman, a crowd that wants an answer, and a prophet asked to rule on the law of Moses. In the Medina report the Prophet holds them to what their own book says. In the John story Jesus turns the question back on the accusers. I find it striking that each tradition kept a story in which a prophet is set a legal trap and refuses to be used by it.
## What a reader should take from it

Read the passage. It is a good story, and its last line, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11), says something true about repentance that the Qur’an also says many times (for example 39:53).

But read it knowing what it is: an early story that found its way into John long after the gospel was written. The rest of John deserves the same question, as the page on John and the Jesus who speaks of himself asks it. The Islamic Dilemma assumes that the four gospels are one fixed text the Qur’an either affirms or denies. John 7:53-8:11 shows that the text itself moved.
For how this compares with the way the Qur’an was handed on, the Abrahamic Religions journal has a piece on the transmission of scripture in all three traditions.
Allāhu aʿlam.
## Sources
- Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994)
- Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3
- Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ

title: Talitha koum: the Aramaic words of Jesus
excerpt: Jesus spoke Aramaic, and the gospels are in Greek. A handful of his words survive untranslated in Mark. Here is what they are and what they tell us about the Injīl.
body: In Mark 5 a synagogue leader named Jairus has a daughter who is twelve years old and dying. By the time Jesus reaches the house, the mourners say she is dead. He takes her by the hand and says two words. Mark writes them down in Aramaic, and then translates them for his readers: “Talitha koum, which means, ‘Little girl, I say to you, arise’” (Mark 5:41).
That small act of translation is worth stopping on. The man in the story spoke one language. The book that tells his story is written in another.
## The words Mark kept
@consensus

Jesus of Nazareth spoke Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee and Judaea in the first century. The four gospels were written in Greek. Mark, the earliest of them, keeps a few of the Aramaic words and glosses each one:
- Talitha koum, “little girl, arise” (5:41).
- Ephphatha, “be opened”, said to a deaf man (7:34).
- Korban, “a gift” dedicated to God (7:11).
- Boanerges, the name given to James and John, “sons of thunder” (3:17).
- Abba, in the prayer at Gethsemane (14:36).
- Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani, “my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (15:34).

Matthew and Luke, who used Mark, drop most of these. Matthew keeps the last but turns Eloi into the Hebrew-sounding Eli (Matthew 27:46). Luke drops all six. The site’s page on the synoptic problem sets out how the three gospels used one another, and this is one of its small signs: the later writers smoothed away what a Greek reader would trip on.
## A language between the lines
So what do the Aramaic words prove? Less than is sometimes claimed, and still something.

No Aramaic gospel survives, and the Syriac Bible (the Peshitta) is a translation from the Greek made centuries later, so it cannot stand in for one. What the words do show is that the tradition Mark worked from still carried the sound of the man’s voice in a few places. Everywhere else, the speech of Jesus reaches us through someone else’s Greek.

One case shows how much can hang on that. Joachim Jeremias argued in the 1960s that abba was a child’s word, “daddy”, and that Jesus used it for God with an intimacy no Jew before him had dared.{{fn:Joachim Jeremias, The Prayers of Jesus (London: SCM Press, 1967), chapter 1, “Abba”.}} The idea spread into a thousand sermons. Then James Barr took it apart in a paper whose title says it all: “Abba isn’t ‘Daddy’.” He showed that abba was the ordinary adult form of address, used by grown men of their own fathers.{{fn:James Barr, “Abba isn’t ‘Daddy’”, Journal of Theological Studies 39 (1988), pages 28-47.}} A large doctrine had been built on a misreading of one word in a language the gospels themselves had already translated.
@minority

Some scholars, Maurice Casey among them, have tried to reconstruct the Aramaic behind whole passages of Mark.{{fn:Maurice Casey, Aramaic Sources of Mark’s Gospel (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998).}} The work is careful and often illuminating. It is still reconstruction: the Aramaic is his, and only the Greek is Mark’s.
## The crowd that misheard
At the cross, Mark says, some of the bystanders heard Eloi and thought he was calling Elijah (15:35). Even in the moment, in his own language, people around him misheard the words.

The site’s position on what happened at the end is set out on the page on the end of his earthly mission, following 4:157-158. Here I only note what the text of Mark itself concedes: the gospel writer translates, the crowd mishears, and Matthew changes the spelling.
## What this means for the Injīl
@islamic

The Qur’an says: “We have not sent any messenger except in the language of his people, so that he may make things clear to them” (14:4). The Injīl that God gave to Jesus (5:46) was given in the language Jesus spoke and preached in. On the site’s reading, set out on what is the Injīl, the Injīl is that message, and the four Greek gospels are later books that carry parts of it.
The Aramaic words in Mark are the closest any reader can get to the sound of that message. There are perhaps a dozen of them. Everything else is translation, and every translation is a reading.

That is a reason to read the gospels closely, which is what this site tries to do. It is also a reason not to build doctrine on a single Greek word that Jesus never said. Barr’s correction of Jeremias is the cautionary tale, and it came from inside Christian scholarship.
The Abrahamic Religions journal has a broader piece on Jesus across the traditions, if you want the wider frame. The glossary here has the Greek and Arabic terms the site uses most.
## Sources
- Joachim Jeremias, The Prayers of Jesus (London: SCM Press, 1967)
- James Barr, “Abba isn’t ‘Daddy’”, Journal of Theological Studies 39 (1988)
- Maurice Casey, Aramaic Sources of Mark’s Gospel (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998)

title: A word from God: kalimah in the Qur’an, logos in John
excerpt: The Qur’an calls Jesus “a word from God”. John calls him the Word who was God. The two phrases sound alike and say opposite things. Here is why.
body: Christian writers have noticed for thirteen centuries that the Qur’an calls Jesus a word from God. John of Damascus, a Christian official at the Umayyad court who wrote in Greek around 730 CE, advised his readers to put it to Muslims directly: if you say Christ is the Word and Spirit of God, how can you call us associators?{{fn:John of Damascus, On Heresies, chapter 100, in Daniel J. Sahas, John of Damascus on Islam (Leiden: Brill, 1972), which gives the Greek with an English translation.}}
It is a fair question, and it deserves a straight answer. The answer is in the verses themselves.
## What the Qur’an says
@islamic

The phrase comes three times. The angels say to Mary: “O Mary, God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary” (3:45). Of John the Baptist the angels tell Zechariah that he will come “confirming a word from God” (3:39). And in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ: “The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say ‘Three’” (4:171).

Read 4:171 again. The same verse that calls Jesus a word from God opens with “only a messenger” and closes by forbidding the Trinity. Whatever the word means, it cannot mean what John of Damascus wanted it to mean, because the sentence that uses it rules that out.

Then 3:59 explains it: “The likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him ‘Be’, and he was.” The word is kun, “Be”. Al-Ṭabarī, commenting on 3:45, gives this as the view of Qatādah, the Successor of Basra: the word “is His saying ‘Be’”.{{fn:Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 3:45, report 7061 (Maʿmar from Qatādah). The site’s translation is on the commentaries on the family of ʿImrān.}} It is one of the readings he records, and it is the one 3:59 supports. Jesus is called a word because he came into being by a word, without a father, as Adam came into being without father or mother.
## What John says
@consensus

John’s gospel opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Greek is logos. Fourteen verses later: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (1:14).

The word logos had a long life in Greek thought before John used it. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who died around 50 CE, wrote of the logos as God’s instrument in making the world, and even called it a “second god”.{{fn:Philo, Questions and Answers on Genesis 2.62.}} Scholars dispute how much John drew from Philo. They agree that the idea of the logos as a divine being standing between God and the world was already in the air.
So John’s Word is a being. It exists before creation, it is with God, it is God, and it takes flesh.
## Two phrases, two directions

Put the two side by side and the difference is plain. The Qur’an’s kalimah is a command God speaks, and Jesus is what that command brought into being. John’s logos is a person who existed before the command, and who became a man.

One makes Jesus the result of God’s creative word. The other makes him the Word himself. The first keeps the line between Creator and creature that the Qur’an never crosses: “Nothing is like unto Him” (42:11). The second crosses it in its first verse.

I think John of Damascus knew this. His advice was a debating move: catch your opponent on a shared word, and hope he does not read the verse it comes from. The move still turns up in modern apologetics, and it still fails on 4:171.
## The hadith that uses the phrase
@islamic

The Prophet used the phrase too, and he used it in a statement of faith. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit reports that he said: whoever testifies that there is no god but God alone, without partner, that Muḥammad is His servant and messenger, “and that Jesus is the servant of God and His messenger, and His word which He cast to Mary and a spirit from Him”, and that Paradise and Hell are real, God will admit him to Paradise.{{fn:Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb aḥādīth al-anbiyāʾ, 3435.}}
The order matters. “Servant” comes first, then “messenger”, then “word”. The word is the third thing said of him, and it is said of a servant.

That is the Jesus of the Qur’an, set out more fully on the page on the Messiah in Islam. The birth by God’s command is on the annunciation and the birth. And the John who wrote “the Word was God” has his own page here, on John and the Jesus who speaks of himself, which looks at why the fourth gospel is so far from the first three.
## A shared word, honestly read
There is real common ground. Both books say Jesus came from God in a way unlike other men, and both tie that to God’s speech. A Muslim can say that sentence and mean it.

Where the two part is the question John 1:1 answers and 4:171 answers the other way: is the word God, or is it something God said? On that, the Qur’an could not be clearer, and it gives the reason in the same breath: “Glory be to Him, that He should have a son. To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth” (4:171).
## Sources
- Daniel J. Sahas, John of Damascus on Islam (Leiden: Brill, 1972)
- Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān ʿan taʾwīl āy al-Qurʾān
- Philo of Alexandria, Questions and Answers on Genesis
- Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ

title: Jesus at prayer: what the gospels record
excerpt: The gospels show Jesus praying alone before dawn, all night on a mountain and face down in Gethsemane. A reader can ask a simple question of every one of those scenes: to whom was he praying?
body: Mark’s first chapter is a busy one. Jesus calls four fishermen, drives out an unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum, heals Simon’s mother-in-law, and by evening the whole town is at the door. Then, Mark says, “rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed” (Mark 1:35).
The disciples have to go and look for him.
## The scenes
@consensus
Every one of the four gospels shows Jesus at prayer, and Luke shows it most. The passages are worth having together, because they are usually read one at a time:
- He prays at his baptism, and it is while he is praying that the heaven opens (Luke 3:21).
- He withdraws to the wilderness to pray, often (Luke 5:16).
- He spends a whole night on a mountain in prayer before he chooses the twelve (Luke 6:12).
- He is praying alone when he asks the disciples who the crowds say he is (Luke 9:18).
- He goes up a mountain to pray, and his face changes as he prays (Luke 9:28-29).
- The disciples watch him pray, and when he finishes they ask him to teach them (Luke 11:1).
- In Gethsemane, “he went a little farther and fell on his face and prayed” (Matthew 26:39). Mark has him fall to the ground (14:35). Luke has him kneel (22:41).
The page on Luke and his sources looks at why Luke adds so many of these. My reading is that Luke wanted his readers to see a man of prayer, and he wrote him that way scene after scene.
## Face down
Look at Matthew 26:39 again. “He fell on his face.” The Greek is epesen epi prosōpon autou. It is the posture of a man who puts his forehead on the ground before someone greater than himself.

A Muslim reading that line knows the posture at once. It is sujūd, the prostration made in every unit of the daily prayer. The Qur’an tells Mary: “O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate, and bow with those who bow” (3:43). It has Jesus say of himself, as a newborn: “He has enjoined on me prayer and almsgiving for as long as I live” (19:31).
So the prayer of Jesus in the gospels and the prayer of Jesus in the Qur’an look alike. On the measure, these passages agree.
## The question the scenes ask

A man who prays is addressing someone. In every scene above, Jesus speaks to God and waits on God. In Gethsemane he asks for the cup to pass and then submits: “not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).
He also refused a title that belonged to God. When a man called him “good teacher”, he answered: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

The Christian answer, settled at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, is that Jesus prayed in his human nature while being God in his divine nature. I want to state that fairly, because it is the answer every Christian reader will give, and it is coherent on its own terms once its premise is granted.
@islamic

The premise is where I part company. The scenes show one man, praying to one God, with his face on the ground, and they say nothing of two natures. To read them as God praying to God, or one nature praying to another, a reader has to bring the doctrine to the text from the outside. Ismāʿīl al-Fārūqī made the point as a rule of knowledge: when reason and revelation seem to conflict, a paradox is never offered as the answer. The plainer reading is the one the Qur’an gives: “Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. That is a straight path” (3:51; 19:36).
## A textual note

Honesty about the text applies here as elsewhere. Luke 22:43-44, the angel who strengthens Jesus and the sweat “like great drops of blood”, is missing from some of the earliest manuscripts, including P75 and Codex Vaticanus.{{fn:Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994), page 151.}} Scholars are divided on whether Luke wrote it. I leave it out of the argument above. The argument does not need it.
The last supper and the night that follows it are compared across the four accounts on the last supper compared.
## Praying as he prayed
I find this the most human picture the gospels give of Jesus. He gets up in the dark because the day will be full. He goes away from the crowd. He kneels, and then he goes lower.

That is what a servant of God does, and it is what the page on who you are as a servant of God asks of every reader. The Qur’an puts it in one line: “The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God” (4:172). The full Qur’anic picture is on the Messiah in Islam.
The Abrahamic Religions journal sets the forms of prayer in Judaism, Christianity and Islam side by side in its piece on prayer across the Abrahamic traditions.
## Sources
- Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994)
- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992)

title: Advent and the return of Jesus
excerpt: Advent began on Sunday with Mark 13 and the coming of the Son of Man. Muslims also wait for Jesus to return. Here is where the two hopes meet, and where they part.
body: Advent began on Sunday 29 November. In the churches that follow the Revised Common Lectionary, this is Year B, and the gospel set for the first Sunday is Mark 13:24-37: the sun darkened, the stars falling, and “the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory” (13:26).{{fn:The Revised Common Lectionary (Consultation on Common Texts, 1992), First Sunday of Advent, Year B.}}
Many people think of Advent as the run-up to Christmas, and it is. It is also, from its first Sunday, about a second coming. The season looks back to a birth and forward to a return.
Muslims wait for a return too. That is less well known among Christians than it should be.
## The return in Islam
@islamic

The Prophet said: “By Him in whose hand my soul is, the son of Mary will soon come down among you as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the swine and abolish the jizya.”{{fn:Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb aḥādīth al-anbiyāʾ, 3448; Muslim, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān, 155.}} A longer report from al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān has him come down by the white minaret east of Damascus, his hands on the wings of two angels, and kill the Dajjāl, the false messiah.{{fn:Muslim, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-fitan, 2937.}}

The Qur’an points the same way. “And he is a sign of the Hour, so do not doubt it” (43:61). And: “There is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death” (4:159). Qatādah, reported by al-Ṭabarī, read “his death” there as the death of Jesus, still to come after his return.{{fn:Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 4:159, reports 10799 and 10800.}}
So both traditions expect Jesus to come back before the end. On that much they agree, and it is worth saying so plainly in a season when Christians are thinking about it.
## Who comes back
They part on who it is that comes back, and why.

In Advent, the one who comes is the Son of Man of Mark 13. The Nicene Creed says he “will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead”, and calls him “true God from true God”. In the hadith, the one who comes is a man: the same servant and messenger who was raised to God (4:158), who comes down to live out his life, to rule by the law, and then to die and be buried. I read the breaking of the cross in the hadith as his own answer to the doctrine built on him, given in person.
The site sets out the Qur’an’s account of how his first mission ended on the end of his earthly mission. The return is the second half of that account.
## The hour he did not know

There is one verse in Advent’s own gospel that a Muslim reader stops at. A few lines after the reading begins, Jesus says: “But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32).
He says he does not know. The knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone, and the man speaking does not have it.
@consensus

The sentence troubled copyists early. Some manuscripts of the parallel in Matthew 24:36 leave out “nor the Son”, and Metzger’s committee judged the shorter text there to be a later change, made because the phrase was hard for later readers.{{fn:Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994), page 51.}} The words stand in Mark.
@islamic

The Qur’an says the same thing about the Hour, and says it of the Prophet Muḥammad too: “They ask you about the Hour, when it will come. Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord. None but He will reveal it at its time” (7:187). Two prophets, six centuries apart, each told to say that he did not know. On the measure, Mark 13:32 is a verse that agrees.
## The delay
Mark 13 has a second hard verse. “Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place” (13:30).

That generation passed. The Christian answers are many: that “these things” means the fall of the Temple in 70 CE, or that “generation” means the Jewish people, or the human race. Each answer has its defenders, and I will not pretend the question is simple.
I think it is enough to note that the Muslim hope never had this problem. The hadith set no date. They describe signs, and leave the time with God, as 7:187 does.
## Waiting well

Advent is a season of waiting, and waiting is something both communities know how to do. The Qur’an does not ask anyone to work out when Jesus will come back. It asks them to be ready to meet God whenever that is.

The signs given to Jesus in his first mission are on the signs, and Mark, whose gospel the churches read through this year, has his own page here: Mark, the first gospel. The dates the site relies on, from the Temple’s fall to the oldest manuscripts, are on the timeline.
Allāhu aʿlam.
## Sources
- Consultation on Common Texts, The Revised Common Lectionary (Nashville: Abingdon Press, 1992)
- Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ
- Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj, al-Ṣaḥīḥ
- Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān ʿan taʾwīl āy al-Qurʾān
- Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994)

title: Hear, O Israel: the first commandment of Jesus
excerpt: Asked which commandment came first, Jesus quoted the Shema: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. Mark keeps the line. Matthew and Luke drop it. A short study of one answer and three gospels.
body: A scribe in Jerusalem had been listening to Jesus argue with the Sadducees, and liked his answers. So he asked one of his own: “Which commandment is the most important of all?” (Mark 12:28).

Jesus did not choose among the 613 commandments the rabbis would later count. He went to the line every observant Jew said morning and evening, and still says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength” (Mark 12:29-30, quoting Deuteronomy 6:4-5).
## The scribe’s reply
What happens next is the part people forget. The scribe answers him back, and he gets it right:

> You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbour as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.
That is Mark 12:32-33. And Jesus, “when he saw that he answered wisely”, said to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (12:34).
So a Jewish scribe says God is one and there is no other besides Him, and Jesus tells him he is close to the kingdom. Jesus asks nothing more of him, about himself or about anything else.
## What Matthew and Luke do with it
@consensus
Most scholars hold that Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source. The page on the synoptic problem lays out the evidence. So it is fair to ask what each of them did with this scene.

Matthew keeps the question and the commandment to love God, and drops the opening line. His Jesus begins: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Matthew 22:37). “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” is gone. So is the scribe’s reply, and so is “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” In Matthew the questioner is a lawyer who asks “to test him” (22:35).

Luke moves the exchange to a different point in the story and gives the answer to the lawyer instead. Jesus asks him what is written in the law, and the lawyer recites the love commandments, again without the Shema line (Luke 10:25-28). Then comes the parable of the good Samaritan.

I do not want to make more of this than it will bear. Matthew’s Jesus is not shy about the law (see Matthew and the law), and no one can prove why a line was dropped. But the fact stands: the one gospel that records Jesus quoting “the Lord is one” is the earliest, and the two that followed it both lost the line.
## The same sentence in the Qur’an
@islamic

A Muslim hears the Shema and recognises it. “Say: He is God, One. God, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there any equivalent to Him” (112:1-4). The scribe’s “there is no other besides him” is close to the first half of the shahādah, lā ilāha illā Allāh.

The Qur’an also tells the Prophet to make exactly this the meeting point with the People of the Book: “Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is equal between us and you: that we worship none but God, and associate nothing with Him, and that none of us take others as lords besides God” (3:64). The Prophet wrote that verse into his letter to Heraclius.{{fn:Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb badʾ al-waḥy, 7.}}

Mark 12:29 and Qur’an 3:64 make the same offer. Ismāʿīl al-Fārūqī read the three Abrahamic faiths as moments of one consciousness, faulted in their historical texts and never in the revelation they began from. This passage is a place where the historical text still shows the revelation plainly.
## And John 17:3

There is one more line, in a very different gospel. In the long prayer of John 17, Jesus says: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (17:3). The only true God, and the one He sent. The verse keeps the two apart in the same sentence.
## What to do with a first commandment

Christian readers often move from Mark 12:29 straight on to the second commandment, love of neighbour, because it is the one that preaches. I understand why. But Jesus put the oneness of God first, and the scribe who heard him repeated it and was praised for it.

That is where the site starts too. The case is made in one page on Why Islam?, and the distance between this Jesus and the theology built on him later is the subject of Paul of Tarsus against Jesus. For the wider history, the Abrahamic Religions journal has a piece on Abrahamic monotheism.
## Sources
- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992)
- Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ

title: Codex Sinaiticus and the oldest complete gospels
excerpt: The oldest complete copy of the four gospels was made in the fourth century and found at a monastery in Sinai. What it contains, what it leaves out, and what it can and cannot prove.
body: In May 1844 a young German scholar named Constantin von Tischendorf was working in the library of St Catherine’s Monastery, at the foot of Jebel Musa in Sinai. He came away with 43 leaves of a Greek Bible, older than anything he had seen. Fifteen years later, on a third visit, a monk showed him the rest of it, wrapped in a red cloth.{{fn:D. C. Parker, Codex Sinaiticus: The Story of the World’s Oldest Bible (London: British Library, 2010).}}
That book is Codex Sinaiticus. It is the oldest manuscript that has the whole of the New Testament, and the oldest complete copy of the four gospels in any language.
## What it is
@consensus

Sinaiticus was copied in the middle of the fourth century, around 350 CE, by at least three scribes. It is written in Greek capitals, four columns to a page, on parchment. It once held the whole Greek Bible. About half of the Old Testament is lost; the New Testament survives entire.{{fn:Parker, Codex Sinaiticus.}}

Its leaves are now in four places. The 43 leaves of 1844 are in Leipzig. The bulk went to the Russian Tsar in 1859, and in 1933 the Soviet government sold it to the British Museum for £100,000. Further fragments turned up in a sealed room at St Catherine’s in 1975. In 2009 the four holders put the whole manuscript online together, at codexsinaiticus.org.

How it left Sinai is still disputed. The monastery holds that the codex was lent and never returned. Tischendorf’s defenders point to a deed of gift signed in 1869. I do not think the evidence settles it.
## What the gospels look like in it
Here is where Sinaiticus matters for this site.

Its Mark ends at 16:8. The women run from the empty tomb “and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” There are no appearances of the risen Jesus, no commission, no ascension. Verses 9 to 20, printed in most Bibles, are not there. Codex Vaticanus, the other great fourth-century Bible, ends Mark in the same place. The accounts of the empty tomb are set side by side on the resurrection accounts compared.
Its John has no woman taken in adultery. John 7:53-8:11 is absent, and the Journal looked at where that story came from in The woman taken in adultery.

And its New Testament has two books that yours almost certainly does not. After Revelation come the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas. The scribes who made the oldest complete New Testament included them as scripture.
## The corrections

Sinaiticus is also one of the most corrected manuscripts there is. The Codex Sinaiticus Project counts about 23,000 corrections, made by many hands from the time it was copied to the twelfth century.{{fn:Parker, Codex Sinaiticus; and the Codex Sinaiticus Project, codexsinaiticus.org, “The corrections”.}} Most are small: spelling, a dropped word, a line copied twice. Some change the reading.
@consensus

I want to be fair here. The great majority of the differences between Sinaiticus and the printed text are minor, and the text of the gospels it carries is, on most pages, the text a modern reader knows. Textual critics treat it as one of their two best witnesses, and they are right to.
## What it can and cannot prove
@islamic

What Sinaiticus cannot do is take us back to the Injīl. It is a Greek book made some 300 years after Jesus, in a language he did not preach in, by scribes who still thought Barnabas and Hermas belonged in it. It shows what the four gospels were in the fourth century. Behind that, the papyri give fragments, and behind the fragments nothing written survives.

That fits what the Qur’an says. The Injīl was given to Jesus (5:46), and the books that came after carry it alongside other things. Sinaiticus shows the second part as plainly as any document could: a Mark that stops at 16:8, a story that is not in John, and two books that did not make the final list.

Compare the Qur’an, whose oldest dated leaves, the Birmingham folios, were carbon-dated in 2015 to between 568 and 645 CE, within the lifetime of the Prophet or close to it. Compelling Evidence has a fuller piece on the preservation of the Qur’an.
The manuscripts of the gospels that the canon left out are on the manuscripts page, and the editions the site uses are in the source library.
Sinaiticus deserves respect. It was made by people who cared about the text, and their work is why we can read it today. Reading it honestly is the best way to show that respect.
## Sources
- D. C. Parker, Codex Sinaiticus: The Story of the World’s Oldest Bible (London: British Library, 2010)
- The Codex Sinaiticus Project, Codex Sinaiticus, codexsinaiticus.org (2009)

title: Peace on the day he was born: Qur’an 19:33
excerpt: In the Qur’an the newborn Jesus speaks from the cradle and asks for peace on the day he was born. Three days before Christmas, a close reading of 19:30-34 and what the baby says first.
body: Christmas is three days away, and the churches will read Luke 2: the shepherds in the field, the angel, and the host of heaven “praising God and saying, ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!’” (Luke 2:13-14).
The Qur’an has its own birth of Jesus, in Sūrat Maryam, and it ends with peace too. But in the Qur’an the one who speaks of peace is the baby.
## The scene

Mary comes back to her people carrying the child. They accuse her: “O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste” (19:28). She says nothing. She points to the child.
They ask how they can speak to an infant in the cradle. Then the infant speaks:

> He said: I am the servant of God. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet. And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined on me prayer and almsgiving for as long as I live, and dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me arrogant or wretched. And peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die and the day I am raised alive.
That is 19:30-33. The English is my own rendering, close to The Clear Quran that the site uses elsewhere. Only the Arabic is the Qur’an.
## The first words
@islamic
The first thing Jesus says in the Qur’an is innī ʿabdu Allāh, “I am the servant of God”.

It is the answer to his mother’s accusers, and it is also the answer to a question that would be asked about him for the next six hundred years. Before he says that he is a prophet, before he says that he has a Book, he says whose servant he is. The Qur’an follows the speech with its own comment: “That is Jesus son of Mary, a statement of the truth about which they dispute. It is not for God to take a son. Glory be to Him. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it ‘Be’, and it is” (19:34-35).
So the Qur’an’s nativity carries its doctrine inside the story. The child names himself, and the verses after name what he is not.
## Peace, twice

Fifteen verses earlier, the same sūrah says of John the Baptist: “And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies and the day he is raised alive” (19:15). Of John, God says it. Of Jesus, Jesus says it of himself, as one who has been given the words to say.

There is a small difference in the Arabic. John is given salāmun, “peace”, without the article. Jesus says al-salāmu, “the peace”. Al-Zamakhsharī, the twelfth-century grammarian of the Qur’an, read the article as pointing back to the peace already spoken over John: the same peace, now given in full.{{fn:Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 19:33.}} It is a fine point, and the commentators disagree about how much to make of it. What is not in doubt is that the two prophets are set side by side, each born by God’s gift against all expectation (John to an old man and a barren wife, Jesus to a mother no man had touched), and each greeted with peace at the three turning points of a human life.
## The three days
@islamic

The three days are a birth, a death and a raising. A Christian reader will hear the shape of the creed in that. A Muslim reader hears something different, and the Qur’an explains it elsewhere: Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, God raised him to Himself (4:157-158), and he will die a natural death after his return. The site sets out the reading on the end of his earthly mission.
On that reading, 19:33 is a prayer for peace on a whole life that is not yet over.
## The cradle in other books
@consensus

The Qur’an is not the only book in which Jesus speaks as a baby. The Arabic Infancy Gospel, a work that goes back to a Syriac original, opens with Jesus in the cradle telling Mary that he is the Son of God and the Word.{{fn:The Arabic Gospel of the Infancy, chapter 1, in Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, editors, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing, 1886).}} The manuscripts of that work are later than the Qur’an, and scholars disagree about the age of the tradition behind it.

So the cradle scene was shared ground. What differs is what the child says. In one, the baby claims to be the Son of God. In the other, the baby says he is God’s servant. The question of whether the Qur’an borrowed its stories is answered at length on did the Qur’an borrow its stories?, and the short answer there applies here: shared material, measured and corrected.
The two gospel birth accounts, Matthew’s and Luke’s, are compared on the birth accounts compared, and the Qur’an’s own account is on the annunciation and the birth.
## At Christmas

Christians will spend this week singing about the birth of Jesus, and Muslims believe in that birth as firmly as they do. It was a miracle, by God’s command, to a virgin (3:47). Mary is the one woman the Qur’an names, and a whole sūrah carries her name. The Abrahamic Religions journal has a piece on Mary across the traditions.
What the Qur’an adds is the baby’s own voice. If you want to know who Jesus said he was, the Qur’an gives his first sentence. “I am the servant of God.” And then: peace on the day I was born.
## Sources
- Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf ʿan ḥaqāʾiq ghawāmiḍ al-tanzīl
- Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, editors, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing, 1886)
- Mustafa Khattab, translator, The Clear Quran

title: Who chose the four gospels?
excerpt: No council picked the four gospels. The record shows second-century teachers arguing for four, and some churches still reading other gospels at the end of that century.
body: Ask when the four gospels became the four gospels and many people answer with a council. The record points elsewhere. In 1877 Samuel Davidson gathered what each Father, list and synod said about the books, and no meeting that chose four opens that record.{{fn:Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), p. 71.}}
What it shows is a slow choice made by teachers in several regions. I follow it in order.
## What the record shows
@consensus

The first known collection of Christian writings in Davidson’s account belongs to Marcion, who came to Rome about 144 with ten letters of Paul of Tarsus and an altered Luke.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 58.}} Davidson makes outsiders the first collectors. I read it more carefully: Marcion left the first known list, and the letters and gospels were already in circulation.

By the second half of the second century Davidson finds a New Testament in two parts, called “the gospel” and “the apostle”. The first part was complete and held the four gospels alone.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 71.}} The singular is worth noticing. For these writers the gospel was one thing, delivered in four books.

Irenaeus supplied the argument for four. In Davidson’s summary he held that “the gospels should be four in number, neither more nor less, because there are four universal winds and four quarters of the world.” The Word, Irenaeus said, “gave the gospel in a fourfold shape.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 79.}} The reasoning is no evidence about who wrote the books. It does show that four had to be argued for.
## Three lists from the same decades

Irenaeus held a collection of four gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, the first letter of John and the Revelation. He kept a lower shelf beside it, which Davidson calls “a sort of appendix or deutero-canon”, and he called one of its books, the Shepherd of Hermas, Scripture.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 71.}}

Clement of Alexandria had a wider appendix again, with Hebrews, Jude, the Apocalypse of Peter, Hermas and the letters of Clement and Barnabas. Davidson says Clement “recognized no obligatory canon, distinct and of paramount authority.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 71.}}

The Muratorian fragment, which Davidson puts about 170 and in Rome, names the four gospels first.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, pp. 72 to 73.}} Its date is contested today, and a fourth-century origin has been argued, so I cite it for its content and leave its date open.
The four gospels are the one fixed point in all three. The books around them differ from teacher to teacher.
## Where the choice was still open

Serapion, bishop of Rhossus in Cilicia, allowed the Gospel of Peter to be read in public at the end of the second century. Davidson draws the conclusion that “there was no exclusive gospel-canon at the end of the second century, at least in Syria.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 74.}}
Tatian’s Diatessaron points the same way. The Syriac churches used his single harmony in place of the four for generations, as the timeline records.

Even the teachers who argued for four did not close the matter. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian agree that the two-part collection existed, and Davidson writes of them: “These three fathers did not fix the canon absolutely.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 72.}}
## Who did the choosing

Davidson names no meeting and no date. He writes: “The conception of canonicity and inspiration attaching to New Testament books did not exist till the time of Irenæus.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 83.}}

He lists what shaped the result. The choice, he says, was “determined by various circumstances, of which apostolic origin was the chief”, together with the example of the churches that first received a writing and the need of teachers to answer heretics with apostolic records.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, pp. 78 to 79.}}

Synods came later. Laodicea in 363, Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 and 419 listed books, and Davidson sums up: “no general council closed the canon once for all, till that of Trent promulgated its decrees.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 120.}}
## What I take from Davidson and what I leave

Davidson wrote in the 1870s. His dates for the gospels and for 2 Peter are later than most scholars now hold, and manuscripts found since his time have changed the picture. I use him for what Fathers and lists said, with page references. I leave his dates and his closing theology aside.
@islamic

The Qur’an speaks of an Injīl given to ʿĪsā (5:46). It speaks of one. The fourfold list came from teachers and synods who chose among writings about him, and the record shows them doing it over generations.

The four still deserve a careful reading. The question for a Muslim reader is the one this site asks on every page: what in these books can be traced back to what was given to ʿĪsā. The method page says how, and the gospels section goes book by book.
## Sources
- Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pages 58, 71 to 72, 74, 78 to 79, 83 and 120
- Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987)

title: Did Nicaea choose the books?
excerpt: The story says the Council of Nicaea voted on the Bible. The old histories of the lists record emperors, teachers and regional synods, and no general council closing the canon before Trent.
body: A story circulates that Constantine called the Council of Nicaea in 325 and that the bishops voted on which books belong in the Bible. The story is told with confidence and rarely with a source.

Davidson’s history of the lists is a good place to test it, because he records what each council said about the books.{{fn:Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pp. 87 to 88, 118 to 120.}}
## What Constantine did
@consensus

Davidson reports that about 332 the emperor Constantine asked Eusebius of Caesarea to prepare a complete collection of the Christian writings for the Church, and that fifty copies were made.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 78.}} He adds that Credner was probably right that the set held every New Testament book except the Revelation.

Davidson is plain about the weight of the order: “No binding authority indeed attached to the list of the Christian books it presented; but it had weight in the Greek Church.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 118.}} Athanasius, who disliked Eusebius and his party, issued a list that included the Revelation.
## The one mention of Nicaea

The Nicene Council appears once in Davidson’s account of the lists. He passes on Jerome’s remark that the book of Judith was “in the number of the books reckoned up by the Nicene Council”.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 87.}} The remark concerns one Old Testament book. It does not describe a vote on the Bible as a whole.

A modern reader will want to know whether the surviving acts of 325 contain any list of books. I have not checked that against a modern edition of the canons, and I would not rest an argument on Jerome’s sentence without doing so.
## The councils that did speak about the books

The Council of Laodicea in 363 forbade the reading of uncanonized books, and its 59th canon allows “only the canonical ones of the New and Old Testament.” Davidson adds that Credner “has proved that this 60th canon is not original, and of much later date”, which means the list of books attached to Laodicea is itself disputed.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 88.}}

The synods of Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 “received the epistle to the Hebrews and the seven general ones, thus fixing the New Testament canon as it now is”, and the African bishops repeated their decision in 419.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 119.}} These were African synods.

The Trullan Council of 692 settled the matter for the Greek Church by a different road. It “did not enumerate the separate books, but referred to older authorities”.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 119.}}
Davidson’s own summary of the synods is short: they “show the view of some leading father like Augustine”.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 87.}}
## Lists that disagreed after Constantine

The Eastern lists went on differing in the generations after the emperor’s order. Davidson notes that the apostolic canons adopted the seven general epistles, while the apostolic constitutions excluded them, and that the Alexandrian manuscript added the two letters of Clement to the usual books.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 118.}}

Athanasius wrote his list of the New Testament books in an Easter letter. Davidson dates it 365, and modern works date it 367, which is the date this site uses. Cyril of Jerusalem and Gregory of Nazianzus gave lists without the Revelation in the same century.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, pp. 89 to 91.}}
## What the story gets right

Councils did matter. Davidson writes that “councils had weight when they enumerated the sacred books”, and he adds that prominent teachers and tradition counted as well.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 120.}}

He names two men as the most influential, Jerome and Augustine, the first holding to the shorter Palestinian list of the Old Testament and the second to the longer Alexandrian one.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 118.}} Between them they left two lists in the Latin Church, and no later voice ended the difference.

He also explains why the story is attractive: “It is the way of men to defer unduly to the opinions expressed by synods and councils, especially if they be propounded dogmatically”.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 120.}}
## The verdict

Davidson ends with a sentence that answers the story directly: “no general council closed the canon once for all, till that of Trent promulgated its decrees.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 120.}} Nicaea set doctrine and church order. The record of the lists comes from emperors, teachers and regional synods over several centuries.
@islamic

The Qur’an asks the People of the Gospel to judge by what God sent down in it (5:47). A Muslim reader who hears that a council voted the books in will ask whether that vote and the Injīl are the same thing. On the evidence, no such vote at Nicaea is on record in this source, and the lists came later and from more than one place.
That leaves the question of the Injīl where this site has always put it, with the manuscripts. The glossary gives the terms, and the timeline sets the lists in order.
## Sources
- Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pages 78, 87 to 88, 118 to 120
- Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987)

title: The 22-book Syriac Bible
excerpt: The Syriac churches nearest Arabia read a New Testament of 22 books. It lacked 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation, and it shows how far the lists differed by region.
body: Count the books of your New Testament and you will probably reach 27. The Syriac Christians of the Near East, whose Aramaic was the language of the churches closest to Arabia, read a New Testament of 22.{{fn:Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pp. 75, 103 to 104.}}
The shorter list is a good reminder that “the canon” never meant one list everywhere.
## What the Peshitta lacked
@consensus

Davidson describes the standard Syriac version: “This work, commonly called the Peshito, wants 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and the Apocalypse.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 75.}} Five books taken from 27 leave 22. It has all the other books, including James and Hebrews, which Davidson says the Syrian church received as apostolic.

He gives the same list elsewhere in different words: “In the New Testament it wanted four of the catholic epistles and the Apocalypse.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 103.}} He adds that the Peshito had only the Hebrew canonical books of the Old Testament at first.
## When it was made

Davidson dates the version to the early third century.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 75.}} Later work puts the Peshitta New Testament in the early fifth century. I give that date with a caution, because it rests on modern studies of the Syriac Bible that a reader should check.
Before it, the Syriac churches had Tatian’s Diatessaron, a single harmony of the four gospels, which the timeline records as the Syriac text of the gospels for generations.
Davidson adds that most of the Apocrypha were translated from the Greek and added later, in what he calls the Nestorian recension.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 103.}}
## Other Syriac witnesses
Davidson is candid about the limits of the evidence: “The history of the canon in the Syrian church cannot be traced with much exactness.”{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 103.}}

Davidson says that Ephrem, whom he dates to 378, cites the Apocrypha as Scripture, and he warns that the quotations come from Ephrem’s Greek works, which have been suspected of tampering.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 103.}}

A later Syriac version, made by Polycarp for Philoxenus of Mabug, carried the four letters the Peshito lacked and, in the Harclean recension of 616, the two letters of Clement. The Apocalypse is still missing.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 104.}}

Junilius, writing about 550 from what a Persian teacher of the school of Nisibis told him, records that “the Apocalypse of John is much doubted by the Orientals”.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 104.}}
## How to read the number

A list of 22 books for the New Testament is a count of what one church read in worship. It is no verdict on the other five. Hebrews, which the Western Church long excluded, and James were received as apostolic in the Syriac list.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 75.}}{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 119.}}

The five missing books are short. Four are brief letters, and the fifth, the Revelation, is the one the Greek lists doubted most often. Davidson shows Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus and Amphilochius leaving it out, and he notes that Junilius found it much doubted in the East.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, pp. 89 to 92.}}

Junilius sorted the books into three grades, those of perfect authority, those added by many, and those added by some. Among the second grade in the New Testament he put James, 2 Peter, Jude, and 2 and 3 John.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 104.}}
## What this shows

The Greek lists of the fourth century and the Latin lists of Hippo and Carthage agreed on 27 books, and a Syriac church of the same period read 22. Churches of one period held two lists, and the difference came from region and usage.

Across the Red Sea the picture was different again. In Davidson’s account the Abyssinian church had at first all the books of the Septuagint together with Enoch, 4 Esdras and Jubilees, and a New Testament that agrees with the present Greek one.{{fn:Davidson, The Canon of the Bible, p. 104.}} Davidson summarised nineteenth-century editions there, so I take it only as a sign that the churches on both sides of Arabia held lists of different lengths.
@islamic

The Qur’an speaks of the Injīl as something given to ʿĪsā (5:46) and addresses the People of the Gospel (5:47). The Christians nearest Arabia read Syriac, and the glossary calls Syriac the likely channel for much of what the Qur’an’s first hearers knew of Christianity.

Which list the Christians of the Hijaz themselves held is not recorded in this source, and I will not guess. What the Syriac Bible does show is that a Muslim reader who asks “which Gospel, and which canon” is asking a question the churches answered in more than one way.
## Sources
- Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible (3rd revised ed., 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pages 75 and 103 to 104
- Sebastian P. Brock, The Bible in the Syriac Tradition (Piscataway: Gorgias Press, 2006)
- Bruce M. Metzger, The Early Versions of the New Testament (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977)
